Without further ado, please enjoy this year’s audiovisual feast: winter in Hulun Buir!

“We used to look up at the sky and wonder at our place in the stars.”

When people ask me my favorite film, Interstellar is definitely part of the answer. Why? A lot of it has to do with one piece from its score, “Cornfield Chase.” Every time I hear this masterpiece of a soundtrack by Hans Zimmer, I see the scene of the spacecraft gliding past Jupiter’s rings: the hero leans against the window, looking out at the enormous rings, the vast ship no more than a lone skiff, and a crushing sense of solitude sweeps over you.


This winter, in Hulun Buir, I felt a little of that solitude. Mention Hulun Buir, the great grassland region in the northeast of Inner Mongolia, and most people picture summer: endless grassland where, as the old folk song goes, the wind bows the grass to reveal the cattle and sheep. Its winter gets talked about far less. Did you know? The coldest place in China isn’t Mohe, the country’s northernmost town, but in Hulun Buir.

Maybe it’s the cold, but there really is hardly anyone here in winter. Driving along the roads through the river valleys, you can go dozens of kilometers without seeing a single car or person. Now and then you spot a little horse foraging in the snow, apparently separated from its herd. Look around and it’s white as far as the eye can see: snow on the left, snow on the right, snow below, and even the sky above looks like snow!

When there’s no wind, all you can hear is the car. Stop and get out, and the stillness is so complete it feels as if the air itself has frozen (at −30°C, it may well have, physically) and sound can no longer travel. You can clearly hear your own breathing. Out on the open plain, it feels exactly like being in a giant, perfect hemi-anechoic chamber, without a single reflection!!!

Sunsets on the grassland are beautiful and long, and in winter the snow makes them unforgettable. The faint red of the setting sun spreads over the snow-covered slopes in the distance and turns them a soft pink.

This drive really did feel a bit like Interstellar, so let’s call the video above “Snowfield Chase – Hulun Buir.” If you’re thinking of going, a friendly reminder: put safety first and prepare properly. Driving on snow is still risky.

Tomorrow is Chinese New Year’s Eve, and many of you are probably on your way home to your families right now. So here’s an early Happy New Year to you all: may all your wishes come true, and may the Year of the Snake bring you luck!
